report.headline: The ACCELERATE trial of evacetrapib was stopped for futility in 12,092 high-risk vascular patients, confirming that CETP inhibition does not reduce cardiovascular events despite massive HDL-C elevation.
report.summary: The ACCELERATE trial randomized 12,092 patients with high-risk vascular disease to evacetrapib 130 mg or placebo, with a primary composite endpoint of CV death, MI, stroke, coronary revascularization, or hospitalization for unstable angina. The trial was stopped early by an independent DSMB on October 12, 2015, for insufficient efficacy after a median follow-up of 1.5 years and 1,670 planned events. Evacetrapib achieved its intended pharmacodynamic effect, raising HDL-C by 129% (non-placebo-adjusted) and 103% (placebo-adjusted) in phase 2, but Mendelian randomization and prior CETP inhibitor failures established that HDL-C elevation is not causal for CVD risk reduction. The modest placebo-adjusted LDL-C lowering of 15% (0.56 mmol/L) yielded an expected hazard ratio of 0.943 with only 22% power, making the trial underpowered even if LDL-C lowering were the sole mechanism. The failure is consistent with the biomarker_not_causal category: the drug's primary mechanism (CETP inhibition → HDL-C elevation) does not translate to clinical benefit.
key_evidence: 12,092 patients randomized (source: Lilly to Discontinue Development of Evacetrapib for High-Risk Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease (Oct 12, 2015))

1,670 planned primary endpoint events (source: Assessment of the clinical effects of cholesteryl ester transfer protein inhibition with evacetrapib in patients at high-risk for vascular outcomes: Rationale and design of the ACCELERATE trial.)

Primary endpoint: composite of CV death, MI, stroke, coronary revascularization, hospitalization for unstable angina (source: Assessment of the clinical effects of cholesteryl ester transfer protein inhibition with evacetrapib in patients at high-risk for vascular outcomes: Rationale and design of the ACCELERATE trial.)
Trial stopped early for futility on Oct 12, 2015, no safety signal (source: Lilly to Discontinue Development of Evacetrapib for High-Risk Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease (Oct 12, 2015))

Phase 2 placebo-adjusted HDL-C increase 103% at 100 mg + atorvastatin (source: Efficacy, safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetic profile of evacetrapib administered as monotherapy or in combination with atorvastatin in Japanese patients with dyslipidemia.)

Phase 3 non-placebo-adjusted HDL-C increase 129% at 130 mg (source: Assessment of the clinical effects of cholesteryl ester transfer protein inhibition with evacetrapib in patients at high-risk for vascular outcomes: Rationale and design of the ACCELERATE trial.)

Placebo-adjusted LDL-C lowering 15% (0.56 mmol/L) in phase 2 at relevant dose (source: Efficacy, safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetic profile of evacetrapib administered as monotherapy or in combination with atorvastatin in Japanese patients with dyslipidemia.)
Calculator predicted 22% probability of success (HR 0.943) based on LDL-C reduction (source: calculator)
CETP genetic association score 0.736 but zero genetic evidence items before 2015-10-12 (source: opentargets:CETP)

No off-target harm: no QT prolongation, no clinically relevant BP effects (source: Effects of the cholesteryl ester transfer protein inhibitor evacetrapib on lipoproteins, apolipoproteins and 24-h ambulatory blood pressure in healthy adults. and Evacetrapib at a supratherapeutic steady state concentration does not prolong QT in a thorough QT/QTc study in healthy participants.)
report.what_would_change_this: A demonstration that CETP inhibition reduces CVD events through a mechanism independent of HDL-C elevation (e.g., via LDL-C/apoB lowering of sufficient magnitude) would be required to alter this conclusion; the ACCELERATE result aligns with the broader CETP inhibitor class evidence that HDL-C raising is not causal.
report.readthrough_note: Other CETP inhibitors show a consistent pattern: torcetrapib increased mortality (off-target toxicity), dalcetrapib was neutral, anacetrapib showed modest benefit (HR 0.91) attributed to LDL-C lowering, not HDL-C raising. The class experience supports that CETP inhibition can confer benefit only via LDL-C/apoB reduction, not HDL-C elevation.

mechanism.target_genetics_rationale: CETP genetic association score 0.736 but evidence_before_cutoff=0 (all 13 Open Targets studies published after 2015-10-12 cutoff). No pre-cutoff genetic evidence for CETP inhibition on coronary disease.
mechanism.notes: LDL-C: Used phase 2 placebo-adjusted combination therapy data (100 mg + atorvastatin 10 mg, 12 wk) per preference (b) - patients on statin background, placebo-adjusted. Verifier questioned whether f_58aadd0f20c7b8 truly represents combination placebo-adjusted data; fact metadata states it does. Dose (100 mg) slightly lower than phase 3 (130 mg). Baseline LDL-C 144.3 mg/dL (3.731 mmol/L) from phase 2. apoB: Only supratherapeutic (600 mg, Day 14) placebo-adjusted data available; no baseline for absolute change. HDL-C: Phase 2 combination therapy placebo-adjusted (100 mg + atorvastatin 10 mg, 12 wk) used; phase 3 data are within-arm only. SBP: Supratherapeutic short-term data (1.69 mmHg at 600 mg, Day 14); phase 2 summary states no clinically relevant BP effect. Follow-up 1.5 years from NEJM publication; trial stopped early for futility with 1670 planned events.

for.text: Evacetrapib raised HDL-C by 103% (placebo-adjusted, phase 2, 100mg+atorvastatin, 12 weeks) and 129% (phase 3, 130mg) — massive on-target biomarker effect.
Mendelian randomization and genetic evidence consistently show HDL-C is not a causal mediator of coronary heart disease; raising HDL-C via CETP inhibition does not translate to CVD benefit.
Prior CETP inhibitors (torcetrapib, dalcetrapib) failed despite large HDL-C increases; anacetrapib's modest benefit in REVEAL was attributed to LDL-C lowering, not HDL-C raising.

hypotheses.would_settle: Consensus from Mendelian randomization studies and the full CETP inhibitor class experience (already established by 2015).

for.text: Placebo-adjusted LDL-C lowering was only -15% (0.56 mmol/L) in phase 2 at the phase 3 dose (100mg+statin); calculator projects expected HR 0.943 (5.7% RRR) with 1.5-year follow-up.
Trial power was only 22% for this effect size; MDE HR for 80% power was 0.872 — far below what LDL-C lowering could deliver.

Phase 3 non-placebo-adjusted LDL-C changes (-14% to -36%) are not reliable for effect sizing; even a true -36% placebo-adjusted reduction would yield only ~12% RRR, still underpowered for 1670 events at 1.5 years.

against.text: If phase 3 placebo-adjusted LDL-C lowering exceeded phase 2 (e.g., -25% to -30%), expected benefit would be larger, though still likely underpowered for the event count and follow-up.

hypotheses.would_settle: Placebo-adjusted phase 3 LDL-C and apoB data at 130mg dose.

for.text: CETP genetic association score 0.736 but with evidence_before_cutoff=0 — no human genetic support for CETP inhibition reducing CVD at the time of trial initiation (2012).

CETP inhibitors have mixed track record: torcetrapib (harm), dalcetrapib (null), anacetrapib (modest benefit via LDL-C), evacetrapib (null). Genetics do not clearly validate CETP as a causal CVD target independent of LDL-C.

against.text: Anacetrapib's REVEAL trial (2017) showed HR 0.91 for major coronary events, suggesting CETP inhibition can confer benefit — but mediated through LDL-C/apoB lowering, not HDL-C raising.

hypotheses.would_settle: Mendelian randomization studies specifically testing CETP variants for CVD outcomes (largely published after 2015).

for.text: Phase 2 supratherapeutic dose (600mg) showed +1.69 mmHg SBP increase (placebo-adjusted, Day 14).

against.text: Phase 2 study concluded evacetrapib was 'devoid of clinically relevant effects on blood pressure' at 600mg.
No QT prolongation at supratherapeutic doses.
Phase 3 safety signal reported as false; no off-target toxicity like torcetrapib's aldosterone/BP effects.

hypotheses.would_settle: Full phase 3 safety dataset (blood pressure, electrolytes, aldosterone).

for.text: High-risk vascular disease population (secondary prevention) — standard population where LDL-lowering therapies show clear benefit.

against.text: No enrichment for low HDL-C or specific dyslipidemia; broad high-risk population appropriate for CVD outcome trial.

hypotheses.would_settle: Subgroup analyses by baseline HDL-C, LDL-C, diabetes status (not available in verified facts).

for.text: Composite endpoint includes coronary revascularization (softer component), but hard components (CV death, MI, stroke) are standard.
Event-driven design with 1670 planned events; stopped early for futility at median 1.5 years follow-up.

against.text: Design similar to successful statin and PCSK9 inhibitor outcome trials; no fatal design flaw.

hypotheses.would_settle: Analysis of hard MACE components only (CV death/MI/stroke).

for.text: Trial stopped early by independent DSMB for 'insufficient efficacy' — a proper execution decision, not an execution failure.

against.text: Large enrollment (12,092 randomized), global conduct, no reported conduct issues.

hypotheses.would_settle: DSMB charter and interim analysis details.

for.text: Phase 3 biomarker data (HDL-C, LDL-C) not placebo-adjusted in verified facts; calculator relied on phase 2 placebo-adjusted data for key inputs.

against.text: Phase 2 placebo-adjusted data at relevant dose (100mg+statin) and duration (12 weeks) available for LDL-C, HDL-C, apoB.
Genetic evidence (CETP score) and class-level CETP inhibitor data provide strong external evidence.

hypotheses.would_settle: Publication of full phase 3 biomarker results with placebo-adjusted changes.

A total of 12,092 patients were randomized to evacetrapib 130 mg or placebo daily in addition to standard medical therapy.

Participants were randomized to 1 of 6 treatment sequences in which they received 1 of 3 treatments: evacetrapib 1200 mg daily for 10 days (supratherapeutic dose), moxifloxacin 400 mg for 1 day (positive control), or placebo for 10 days in each of the 3 separate treatment periods.
Phase: PHASE3
